title: Sample Size and Statistical Power
subtopics: Type I and Type II errors
learning_outcomes: Explain sample size and statistical power and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of sample size and statistical power to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study sample size and statistical power in the context of statistical inference, experimentation, and causal analysis. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Sample Size and Statistical Power matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Inference and experiments quantify uncertainty around comparisons. Statistical significance, causal identification, and practical value are distinct ideas.

items.title: Effect size
items.text: Define effect size in relation to sample size and statistical power; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Variance assumptions
items.text: Work through variance assumptions using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Type I and Type II errors
items.text: Check the edge cases for type i and type ii errors: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Power calculations
items.text: Document the rule or choice for power calculations so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Minimum detectable effects
items.text: Define minimum detectable effects in relation to sample size and statistical power; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by sample size and statistical power. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Predefine outcomes, inspect randomization, plan sample size, and report uncertainty.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Inference and experiments quantify uncertainty around comparisons. Statistical significance, causal identification, and practical value are distinct ideas. task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.

Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
